schools.summary: Henry anatomizes the sin — disobedience to Deut. 7:3, the profaned crown of Israel's peculiarity, a carnal distrust of God, and children exposed to idolatry — and lays the chief guilt on the princes and rulers.
Keil and Delitzsch survey the whole chapter: the princes' report of mixed marriages, Ezra's astonishment till the evening sacrifice, and his confession in the congregation's name.
Gill sets the scandal 'when these things were done,' just after the returned exiles had settled their affairs.
Clarke identifies the offenders as Zerubbabel's returnees, found little better than the Canaanite nations.

themes: mixed marriages with the peoples of the land
priests and rulers chief in the trespass
disobedience to the law of separation

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read Ezra's torn garments (Josh. 7:6) and plucked hair (Neh. 13:25) as signs not of mourning (Job 1:20) but of violent moral indignation, leaving him 'stunned' and motionless.
Gill shows the corruption spreading through every rank — widowers, sons, and even married men taking heathen wives.
Clarke presses that the 'first men,' the rulers, were the most capital offenders, reaching for Virgil to catch how a leader's guilt outweighs the rest.

themes: the rulers foremost in the sin

schools.summary: Clarke sets the rending of garments among all ancient nations and reads the plucked hair — sharper than the shaven head of grief — as abhorrence of the marriages and the idolatry joined to them.
Henry reads Ezra's astonishment as sorrow for the dishonour done to God and the people's danger — holy sorrow great as for an only son, amazed at the scandalous sins of professors.
Gill notes the rending of both inner and outer garment as a double token of grief.

themes: astonishment at the sins of professors

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the gathering of the God-fearers as prompted by the exiles' transgression, Ezra sitting astonished till the evening sacrifice.

Clarke times the evening sacrifice as the last offering of the day and pictures Ezra withdrawn in some secret part of the temple; Wesley marks the hour when the people assembled and the duty of standing with those who act for God.
Gill describes the assembled as those who revered God's word and dreaded his judgments.

themes: those who trembled at God's word

schools.summary: Henry dwells on the evening sacrifice as a type of the great propitiation, the Lamb of God (recalling Gabriel to Daniel, Dan. 9:21), and reads the kneeling and outspread hands as intercession — a confession of the people's sin, not his own.

Clarke reads the kneeling as deepest humility and the spread hands as laying hold on mercy; Wesley marks the change from a mourner's to a petitioner's posture, with an eye to the propitiation the sacrifice typified.
Gill takes 'rose from my heaviness' of rising from the ground and from a day's fasting.

themes: the evening sacrifice as type of Christ

schools.summary: Henry expounds iniquities risen over the head and grown to heaven like the sin of Sodom, yet God's mercy is in the heavens (Ps. 36:5); holy shame is as needful as holy sorrow, the penitent most ashamed when he lifts his face to God (Luke 18:13).
Keil and Delitzsch trace the prayer's argument from shame at the greatness of the guilt, through past punishment, to the fresh transgression.
Clarke hears the shame of a backslider ashamed to seek mercy again; Wesley marks the 'our' by which Ezra owns a guilt now become national.
Gill notes the prayer opens 'O my God' in covenant faith.

themes: ashamed to lift up the face

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch spell out the delivering to sword, captivity, and 'confusion of face' (Dan. 9:7), and read 'as it is this day' of a suffering still present under foreign rule.
Henry makes the fathers' example an aggravation, not an excuse, and reads a people 'brayed in the mortar' yet unreformed (Prov. 27:22), fearing the measure of iniquity nearly full.
Gill hears in 'since the days of our fathers' the aggravation of a long-continued sin.
Wesley: the guilt of the fathers is unpurged, its effects still felt, its sins repeated.

themes: sin since the days of the fathers

schools.summary: Henry orders the mercy — its time ('a little space'), its fountain (God's free grace), its streams (a remnant, a nail, the house of God), and its effect (enlightened eyes, revived hearts) — and turns it against the ingratitude of sinning again.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'a little moment' (Isa. 26:20) of grace against long ages of suffering, the 'rescued remnant' the community returned from Babylon.

Clarke reads the grace as God swaying the Persian kings, the nail as ground for a tent-peg, the reviving as a new trial begun with little; Wesley takes the nail as a settlement, the bondage as continuing subjection.
Gill notes how soon the people relapsed after so recent a favour.

themes: a nail in the holy place

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch unfold the mercy shown to bondmen — reviving, the house of God rebuilt, and 'a wall in Judah and Jerusalem.'
Henry prizes the restored temple worship as the sweetest stream of mercy — blessed are those who dwell in God's house, who call it 'my rest for ever.'
Wesley reads the 'wall' as the favour of the Persian kings and the providence of God, a wall of protection, not of stone.
Gill fixes the frank confession 'we were bondmen' to the Chaldeans.

Henry makes the verse an anatomy of amazement — true penitents at a loss what to say, unable to plead innocence, payment, or despair, taught at last to say 'God be merciful to me a sinner' (Hos. 14:2).
Keil and Delitzsch turn the question into the doorway of confession: we can say nothing but that we have forsaken thy commandments.
Clarke sharpens the timing — the people provoke God anew in the very beginnings of mercy.
Gill hears the cry of a people who can find no apology for such ingratitude.

themes: what shall we say after this

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch guard the citation as a faithful summary, not a verbal quotation — the prohibition of intermarriage inculcated by Moses and the prophets alike.
Clarke reads 'filled from one end to another' as a sweeping torrent of abomination covering the whole land.
Gill names Moses, Joshua, and the prophets as the servants through whom the charge came.

themes: the covenant terms of the land

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch tie the prohibition's promise ('that ye may be strong') to secure inheritance, and set it as the hinge of Ezra's mounting argument that a fresh breach must bring extirpation.
Gill fixes the command as the old law of separation of Deut. 7:3.
Wesley draws the paradox — the alliances men thought would strengthen would in truth weaken and ruin them.
Henry presses the paradox that God punished less than they deserved (against Isa. 40:2's 'double'), so that to sin again would be to run up a new score and turn grace into wantonness.
Clarke marvels that the calamities, as temporal punishments, were far less than the provocations deserved.
Gill lists the judgments — famine, sword, pestilence, captivity — visited for Israel's idolatries.

themes: the fear of a new debt

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence to its trembling end — a relapse after such sparing could leave no remnant nor escaping.
Henry reads the holy fear: no surer presage of ruin than revolting to the same sins after great judgments and deliverances — a people fit to be rejected as reprobate silver (Jer. 6:29).
Gill names the nations of 'these abominations' as guilty of idolatry and all uncleanness.

themes: should we break thy commandments again

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the appeal to God's righteousness not as a plea for pardon but as a warning to the conscience — a justice that had spared only a remnant and could justly consume.

Clarke shades 'righteous' toward mercy (the righteousness of Rom. 3:25 that remits past sins), the ground the remnant escaped; Wesley reads the self-arraignment of men who must fall before God's tribunal.
Gill: God would be just even should Israel be utterly consumed.

debates.question: In what sense is God called 'righteous' at the prayer's close?

sides.position: His justice, which would be vindicated even in consuming Israel, invoked to rouse the conscience
His mercy — the righteousness that spares a remnant and remits past sins (Rom. 3:25)
